name: A Perfect Hard-Boiled Egg
headnote: A short technique piece rather than a true recipe: nail the method once and you get hard-boiled eggs with a creamy, evenly set golden centre every time. Eggs and a teaspoon of salt are the whole ingredient list. NYT frames it as the foundation for a whole run of egg dishes, and it sits inside their larger guide to cooking eggs.
comment_digest: The notes are mostly a running argument about method. The top note (391 votes) says it has never found a reliably peelable egg with this approach and points to a steaming method instead. Another high-voted note (164) challenges the recipe directly: if the eggs sit in the cooking water for two hours, won't you get the grey ring around the yolk? Several readers post competing procedures - cover cold eggs with cold water, bring to a boil, cook 10 minutes, dump the hot water, refill with cold, then crack all over and roll between the palms so the shell slips off (113 votes); an 80-year-old reader (58) swears by lowering eggs into already-boiling water with a teaspoon of vinegar. One widely-agreed practical point (40 votes): fresh eggs will not peel cleanly no matter what trick you use, so buy them a week ahead.
flags: strong reader disagreement with the author's method; peeling is the recurring complaint

name: All-Purpose California Beef Rub
headnote: A dry rub built on the salt-pepper-garlic backbone of Santa Maria barbecue, deepened with ground coffee and clove so the flavour is hard to identify until you say what's in it. It suits both grilling and roasting. The recipe scales up easily and the mix keeps well in a sealed jar or zip-top bag. Give it at least two hours on the meat, and overnight if you can.
comment_digest: The single most-endorsed tip (256 votes, repeated by another commenter at 44) is to coat the beef in soy sauce and let it dry slightly before applying the rub, so the spices grip and the crust is better. A 121-vote note simply transcribes the proportions for people who want them at a glance: roughly 2 Tbsp ground coffee, 1 Tbsp each coarse salt, garlic powder and brown sugar, 1 tsp pepper, and a quarter teaspoon each of cayenne, clove and cinnamon. Several cooks leave the brown sugar out entirely and report it is still excellent on cheap tri-tip. The recurring confusion is quantity: the batch makes far more than one tri-tip needs, and commenters ask without agreement how much actually belongs on the meat. It is also praised on steak and flank, with a fruit salsa playing off the coffee.
flags: no clear guidance on rub quantity per pound - readers disagree

name: Almond Biscotti (Cantucci Di Prato)
headnote: Domenica Marchetti's take on the classic Prato biscotti - crisp, dry and lightly perfumed with almond, close to the original Italian version. The Post tested it both ways and preferred the crumb from a stand mixer, though you can mix by hand: mound the flour, well the centre, add everything else and draw the flour in from the edges like pasta dough, then finish kneading by hand. They keep for about two weeks in an airtight container at room temperature. Adapted from her book Ciao Biscotti.
flags: Washington Post, not NYT - the site has no reader comments/notes section, so only the headnote and rating (3.1 from just 8 ratings, a thin sample) were available; ingredient list does give gram weights

name: Almond Cake
headnote: Adapted by Bittman and Sifton from Molly Wizenberg of Orangette, this is a damp, aromatic olive-oil cake built on a whole boiled orange and lemon plus ground almonds. There is some work up front - you need a food processor and a mixer, and the citrus has to be boiled and pureed and the nuts ground - but the ingredient list is short and the batter comes together quickly once that is done. Good plain, better still with poached pears or grilled figs.
comment_digest: By far the most-voted notes are questions about technique rather than praise. The top note (823) argues the recipe is really an almond-flavoured wheat cake and recommends a Spanish version using all almond flour and eight eggs instead of four for a genuine almond cake. The second (729 votes) flags the instruction as ambiguous: what exactly counts as the pulp you discard, and does that include the rind? The community answer, repeated at 219 and 170 votes: boil both fruits whole, then for the lemon scoop out the insides and keep only the rind, while for the orange keep everything but the seeds. The other frequent ask (309 votes) is substituting almond flour for whole nuts; the answer given, at 397 votes, is about 1 1/2 cups plus 2 tablespoons.
flags: recipe wording on discarding lemon/orange pulp is genuinely unclear - the comments are the fix

name: Basic Dough for Fresh Egg Pasta
headnote: David Tanis is upfront that fresh pasta takes practice - only repetition teaches you what the dough should feel like under your hands and how thin to take it. A hand-crank machine is perfectly legitimate and well suited to a small batch; you do not have to roll by hand. But it is not difficult work, and most reasonably confident home cooks will get there without ever rivalling an Italian nonna. The payoff is that homemade egg pasta beats anything boxed.
comment_digest: The most-voted notes are about feel and rest, not ingredients. The top note (155 votes) adds a step the recipe omits: rest the dough after mixing, then rest it again partway through rolling for at least five minutes, which relaxes the gluten and gives noticeably better sheets. A close second (144) describes the target texture - silky with a definite springiness - and says learning that is the real skill. A 108-vote note gives the Italian baseline ratio every child there knows: 100 g of 00 flour, a pinch of salt and one large egg per person, with an extra yolk if you want it richer. Others offer variants: half all-purpose and half semolina at twice the flour weight to egg weight (about 52 g of each per egg). A practical warning: hold back some flour and add it only if needed, or humidity can leave you with a cornmeal-like texture.
flags: useful gram ratios in comments (100 g 00 flour : 1 egg) for the weights conversion

name: Biscotti Cioccolato
headnote: No headnote on the page - the recipe carries only a Linda Wells byline and a note that it ran with the 1989 pieces Living With Style and Crumbs in the Covers. Commenters identify it as an old Maida Heatter recipe. It is a chocolate-and-almond biscotti that has been a Christmas fixture for NYT readers since it was first printed.
comment_digest: Only ten notes, and vote counts are in single digits, so nothing here is strongly validated. The most-endorsed (8 votes) calls it the family go-to and suggests two changes: sliced almonds rather than whole, because the baked logs are much easier to slice, and more espresso powder than called for. Another commenter reports Milk Street runs essentially this recipe but bumps the chocolate to 8 oz, cuts the almonds, and adds a cup of roasted pistachios and half a cup of dried cherries. Two long-time makers, one since the 1989 article, stress shelf life: packed in a tight tin or glass jars they keep for a long stretch, which is why they work as gifts. One substitutes a cup of finely grated semisweet chocolate.
flags: no headnote exists on the page; only 10 comments with very low vote counts

name: Braised White Beans and Greens with Parmesan
headnote: A weeknight riff on the Roman pairing of puntarelle with white beans. Canned beans keep it fast, and Swiss chard stands in for the chicory - far easier to find in the States and much less bitter - though kale or escarole slot in just as well. Pecorino Romano sharpens the broth more than Parmesan does, but either is fine. Ladle it into shallow bowls with toasted country bread for the garlicky liquid.
comment_digest: The single most-voted note (2,498) is a correction: do not discard the chard stalks. Treat chard as two vegetables, cut the stalks out, dice them and start them early with the aromatics so they soften alongside. Fennel substitutions are the next big theme (1,350 votes): leeks for a milder result, with celery reserved for raw applications rather than this braise. An 815-vote note encourages going well beyond chard - dandelion, turnip, beet and collard greens, arugula, even foraged spring greens all work. Bacon is a popular protein addition (777), and several people report the dish is even better as leftovers, thinned into a soup or spooned over toast. The recipe is one of the site's most-reviewed at over 19,000 ratings.
flags: top comment contradicts the recipe's handling of chard stalks

name: Broccoli and Cheddar Soup
headnote: Alison Roman's version of the fast-casual chain standard, which has built an outsized online following. It is thickened with a roux, so it comes out heavier than a cream of broccoli, and you can blend it entirely smooth or leave it coarse and rustic. The one non-negotiable is the cheese: use the sharpest Cheddar you can get, orange or white, since that sharpness supplies both richness and the acidity the soup needs.
comment_digest: The highest-voted note (531) reports the soup works fine with whole milk in place of the cream and an ordinary supermarket sharp Cheddar, so the dairy is flexible. Just behind it (507 votes) is a widely-liked addition: chop a carrot in, both because the soup looks drab otherwise and because the faint sweetness plays off the broccoli. A related trick (358) is to add a potato and puree it in for body when you are skipping the half-and-half. Bacon appears often (164) - render it first, cook the onion and garlic in the fat instead of butter, and scatter it back over the top. Smaller but consistent flavour tweaks: a teaspoon of Colman's English mustard and a pinch of red pepper flakes, with commenters cutting the final salt addition.

name: Broiled Chicken Breast Salad with Curry Dressing--Franey
headnote: There is no headnote on the page - the recipe carries only the tag that it ran in Pierre Franey's 60-Minute Gourmet column, so no descriptive text exists to paraphrase. It is a warm salad of broiled chicken breast dressed with a curry vinaigrette, from Franey's fast-weeknight series.
comment_digest: Only two notes, with one vote between them, so there is essentially no reader consensus to report. One commenter says it has been a family favourite for thirty years. The other, who made it when it first ran, calls the result astounding and attributes it to the contrast between the hot broiled chicken and the cool dressed greens; they suggest grilling rather than broiling the chicken, with a contrasting marinade, would improve it further. Nothing here corrects quantities, timings or technique.
flags: no headnote exists; only 2 comments and 17 ratings - very thin page

name: Butter-Braised Asparagus
headnote: A deliberately plain treatment for the first asparagus of spring: butter, lemon and delicate herbs, nothing more. The one step the recipe insists on is peeling the stalks, which it says changes the texture substantially. It ran alongside a piece on asparagus being at its sweetest in spring.
comment_digest: The top note (101 votes) is about waste: microwave the trimmed-off ends, puree them, enrich with butter and seasoning, and serve that as a buttery sauce beside the spears. The next (79) invokes Julia Child in support of peeling medium and large spears, but disputes the usual prep - do not snap the spears at their natural break point, line them up and cut about half an inch off instead, which wastes far less. A 49-vote note gives a peeling technique: press the spear flat on a board with one hand and shave with the other. A dissenting 40-vote note prefers Patricia Wells's braise - wash but do not dry the spears and braise in 2 to 3 tablespoons of butter per pound and a half, no peeling. One commenter questions trimming the ends at all.
flags: readers disagree on whether to peel and on snapping vs cutting the ends

name: Buttermilk Roast Chicken
headnote: Nigella Lawson's spatchcocked roast chicken, which reads as casual as barbecue without any of the work. Butterflying the bird takes nothing more than kitchen shears. The buttermilk - normally a fried-chicken ingredient - both tenderises the meat and carries the rosemary, pepper and garlic deep into it, so the aromatics register properly. Maple syrup substitutes for the honey if you prefer. The marinating bird will happily sit in the fridge for up to two days, getting more tender, so dinner is just a matter of putting it in the oven.
comment_digest: The most-endorsed change (616 votes) is to stop discarding the marinade drippings and instead roast the chicken over sliced potatoes in a cast-iron pan so they soak up the juices, which also removes the need for a rack. A 338-vote note extends this: add carrots and halved Brussels sprouts around the bird about 20 minutes into the roast. A 254-vote question - rack or straight onto foil - goes unresolved by the recipe itself. Thighs work well in place of a whole bird (249 votes), and that commenter used 2 tablespoons of honey and found the rosemary did not dominate. Practical tip at 169 votes: crush the peppercorns between a towel or heavy paper with a mallet, checking often since they pulverise fast. Maple syrup is the common swap.
flags: recipe is ambiguous about rack vs. direct pan - a highly-voted question with no author answer

name: Caramelized Onion and Fennel Risotto
headnote: A substantial autumn risotto whose flavour comes from onions and fennel cooked down until caramelised. It was submitted by a reader, Joe DiMaria of Somerville, who wanted a vegetarian holiday main that did not fall back on squash, root vegetables or sweet potatoes - the usual default, and one he does not like. NYT ran it as part of a vegetarian Thanksgiving series.
comment_digest: Vote counts here are low (top note 42), so treat the advice as suggestive. That top note warns the fennel comes through only faintly while the herbs, rosemary in particular, are assertive and should be dialled back. A 16-vote note is blunter: the recipe works but only if you ignore parts of it, singling out the 25 to 30 minute caramelisation over medium-high heat as far too aggressive for most pans. Several cooks scale the rice down to one cup while keeping a full onion and fennel bulb, which shifts the ratio toward the vegetables - one specifies 1 tablespoon rosemary, one onion, one bulb, one cup rice, finished with lemon juice to brighten it. Going heavy on onion and fennel with a punchy olive oil is a recurring endorsement.
flags: low vote counts throughout; commenters say the stated caramelisation heat and time are wrong

name: Cauliflower Gratin with Leeks and White Cheddar--Alison Roman
headnote: Alison Roman's shortcut gratin: no blanching the cauliflower and no bechamel to make. The cauliflower and leeks go into the dish with cream and bake under foil, which steams them tender without letting them dry out. Pulling the foil off for the rest of the bake browns the top and reduces the cream into a thick, glossy sauce on its own. If you want crunch, scatter olive-oil-tossed, seasoned bread crumbs over it at the point the foil comes off.
comment_digest: The most-voted note (249) is a leek-cleaning technique rather than a recipe change: cut an X into the base and stand the leek in a bowl of water for five to ten minutes so the grit falls out. The dominant substantive thread is dairy substitution, which the recipe does not address - a 242-vote question asks for an alternative to heavy cream and whether it freezes, and readers answer from experience: coconut milk changed neither flavour nor texture (205 votes), half-and-half works (134), and plain Greek yogurt works when doubled, though with a looser result (107). Cheese is equally flexible - Gruyere and Parmesan in place of cheddar, and an onion standing in for the leek, drew 175 votes. Bread crumbs on top are near-universally recommended.
flags: top-voted question about cream substitutes goes unanswered by the recipe; readers supply the answers

name: Charlie Bird's Farro Salad
headnote: Melissa Clark argues a farro salad lives or dies on two things: seasoning the grain properly as it cooks, and using genuinely good olive oil in the dressing. This one, from Ryan Hardy at Charlie Bird in SoHo, does both. The farro simmers in apple cider with bay leaves and a lot of salt until it is worth eating on its own, then gets heavily dressed with oil and enriched with pistachios and Parmesan. Tomatoes, radishes, arugula and a mass of herbs are folded in at the last minute to lift it.
comment_digest: The highest-voted note (979) resolves the recurring cooking-time complaints: pearled and unpearled farro behave completely differently and the recipe does not say which to use, so timings vary wildly - a follow-up at 463 votes prefers unpearled for texture. With Trader Joe's 10-minute farro, one widely-endorsed adjustment (692 votes) is 1 cup cider plus 1 cup water, simmered only 15 minutes, with the olive oil cut back. If you have no cider (579 votes), use half to three-quarters of a cup of apple cider vinegar with 1 to 2 tablespoons honey topped up with water to 3 cups total. Multiple cooks (542) say the salt in the farro is excessive once the Parmesan goes on. One 469-vote note corrects a common misreading: it is apple cider, not vinegar.
flags: recipe does not specify pearled vs. unpearled farro - the single biggest source of reader failure; salt level disputed

name: Chicken and Orzo Soup with Leeks, Peas and Asparagus
headnote: Ann Maloney's spring adaptation of a chicken soup from America's Test Kitchen's The Chicken Bible, written for cold spring days when you still want the season's produce. The broth gets its character from thinly sliced leeks, celery and a little dried thyme; carrots and peas go in for colour and sweetness, and the asparagus goes in near the end so it keeps some bite. Cooked chicken - poached, or leftover, light or dark meat - is shredded in at the finish. She praises it mainly as a way to use up odds and ends of vegetables and cut waste.
flags: Washington Post article page, not NYT; the site shows a comment count (17) but no readable notes/reviews section on the recipe, so no comment digest could be built; no star rating displayed

name: Chicken in Mustard Sauce
headnote: A Jacques Pepin dish that ran in the Times in 1988 - light but polished, and quick enough for a weeknight at roughly half an hour. Brown the chicken, then build a fast sauce from onions, water and mustard and reduce it until it thickens. Rice is the suggested partner so nothing is wasted, with a sharp green salad alongside. Boneless thighs substitute happily for breast if you add a little extra cooking time.
comment_digest: The comments are largely a collective rewrite of the sauce. The top note (667 votes) flours the chicken first, removes it, then cooks the onion with sliced mushrooms and garlic before deglazing. A 352-vote note is openly critical - it says plenty of readers find the dish flat and blames the water, recommending broth, white wine and/or lemon juice in its place. That substitution recurs throughout, often alongside doubling the mustard and using both Dijon and stone-ground (66 votes). Garlic and additional herbs are the other standard additions. A dissenting 98-vote note says skip the flouring step entirely as unnecessary, and suggests honey, apricot jam or cardamom in the sauce. A 130-vote defender likes it as written for its richness without cream.
flags: substantial reader disagreement with the author - many find the water-based sauce bland and swap in stock or wine

name: Chicken Spaghetti
headnote: A Southern potluck and picnic casserole: creamy, cheesy noodles bound with chicken, tomatoes and chiles, buried under more cheese and baked till it bubbles. The dish has drifted a lot over the years - some versions lean on Velveeta and canned cream of mushroom, and Craig Claiborne's own childhood recipe added a quarter pound each of ground beef and pork to a whole chicken. This one drops the canned soup for a roux thickened with milk and stock, and uses Cheddar with Parmesan. Any cooked chicken works, from leftover roast to rotisserie.
comment_digest: Vote counts are modest, so nothing is heavily validated. The clear leader (132 votes) is a flavour fix: boil the spaghetti in chicken broth rather than water and use a cup of that cooking liquid where the recipe calls for liquid - the commenter says it transforms the dish. Sour cream stirred in is the next most-endorsed addition (56 votes) for a smoother, creamier result. Others double the garlic and use fresh chopped tomatoes in place of canned. Several note the close kinship to chicken tetrazzini, the difference being the tomatoes and green chiles. One variation swaps the spaghetti entirely for taco-flavoured corn chips. A few remark on how dated the onion and garlic powder feel, and report it freezes well in portions.
flags: low vote counts; no strong corrections to quantities or timings

name: Chicken Tortilla Soup
headnote: A weeknight take on sopa de tortilla, the central Mexican classic built on a clear chicken broth flavoured with pureed roasted tomatoes, chiles and garlic and finished with fried tortilla strips. Here the tomatoes, onion, garlic and chile go under the broiler on a foil-lined sheet pan, which does the charring with almost no cleanup. It takes well to additions - sliced zucchini or epazote with the chopped tomatoes, or corn kernels stirred in at the end - and swapping cooked black beans for the chicken makes it vegetarian. A slow-cooker version exists separately.
comment_digest: The two highest-voted notes (177 and 122) both shortcut the broiling step with canned fire-roasted tomatoes - either one 28-ounce can or two 14-ounce cans - instead of fresh plum tomatoes. The 122-vote note goes further and skips the cherry-tomato salsa garnish altogether, finishing instead with shredded cabbage, sour cream, sliced radish and avocado. Against that, a 29-vote note from someone who has made a lot of tortilla soup says the sheet-pan roasting is the whole point and is worth keeping. Ordinary tomatoes work fine if that is what you have (48 votes), with cilantro blended into the salsa. Smaller suggestions: build the broth yourself from bone-in skin-on thighs and vegetable scraps, add more tomato paste, and use rotisserie chicken.
flags: readers split on whether to broil fresh tomatoes or use canned fire-roasted

name: Chicken-Tarragon Pot Pie
headnote: Julia Moskin's adaptation of a recipe from Julia and Jacques at Home, which ran with a Times piece on roast chicken. It is designed around leftovers and works just as well with what is left of the Thanksgiving turkey. Rich, but loaded with vegetables. Dried tarragon can stand in for fresh, though use less than a tablespoon and taste as you go.
comment_digest: The top note (411 votes) addresses a soggy bottom: use a double crust, and brush the raw bottom crust with egg white before the filling goes in to seal it. A 205-vote note found the crust troublesome, went back to the Child and Pepin original, and reports the source recipe calls for only half a batch of crust and bakes in an oval eight-cup dish - a real discrepancy with the NYT version. Another well-liked tip (289) is to chill poultry stock overnight, lift the solidified fat off and use it in the pastry for deeper flavour. On the filling, 251 votes confirm 2 percent milk substitutes for the cream without problems. A 207-vote note is candid about using store-bought crust and treats the recipe as a template for any pot pie. Season the filling generously.
flags: crust quantity appears to differ from the Child/Pepin original - flagged by a 205-vote commenter

name: Chili Verde
headnote: No headnote on the page - the recipe is tagged only as having run in Pierre Franey's 60-Minute Gourmet column, so there is no descriptive text to paraphrase. Commenters identify it as a pork chili verde from one of Franey's one-hour cookbooks, written around a pressure cooker to hit the time limit.
comment_digest: Only fifteen notes and low vote counts, so the guidance is suggestive rather than settled. The most-voted (25) says the pressure cooker is unnecessary - long, slow cooking gets you the same place. A 17-vote note raises a definitional objection to the recipe itself: if it contains tomatoes it is not chili verde at all but chili rojo, and should be a separate recipe. Practical amendments from lower-voted commenters: use pork shoulder rather than tenderloin, which the recipe's timing tends to dry out; oven-simmer covered for about three hours, break the pork up, add the cilantro, then another 45 minutes uncovered to reduce; or pressure-cook and shred the pork while the sauce reduces. One family compares it to green pozole with hominy added.
flags: no headnote exists; only 15 comments; a commenter disputes that the recipe is chili verde at all
